<reason>Side B wins by building a stronger case on the decisive clash of accessibility and ordering. While Side A effectively argues that physical spaces prevent loneliness at its source and that digital platforms risk becoming substitutes, Side B more successfully demonstrates that prioritizing physical infrastructure first structurally excludes commuters, night-shift workers, parents, and anxious or immunocompromised students during the implementation gap. Side B's rebuttals were sharper, directly answering the pressure questions about construction timelines and the "bridge" mechanism with the contrast between digital noticing missed check-ins versus physical spaces only noticing after repeated attendance. Side B's closing framing of "selection vs. prevention" crystallized the choice more decisively than Side A's "manage vs. prevent" dichotomy, giving B a clearer path to victory on the proposition as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2, specifically the A1/A2 answers to Side A's Pressure Questions: B4.1 ("The bridge is in the design, not in anonymous scrolling") directly neutralized A's claim that digital platforms inevitably become substitutes, while B4.6 ("A platform can notice a missed check-in... while a room notices only after repeated attendance") undermined A's argument about physical spaces providing superior accountability and care, exposing a real weakness in A's accessibility case.</best_rebuttal>
